voice.text: A big puddle sits by the gate in the morning. [pause] By lunchtime, it is gone. [pause] Where did the water go? Tap your guess.

Meet one little water drop in the sea. [pause] The sun heats it, and heats it — until the drop rises into the air as an invisible gas. [pause] That is <emphasis>evaporation</emphasis>: liquid water turning into gas.

High in the sky it is cold. [pause] The cold turns the gas back into tiny liquid droplets. That is <emphasis>condensation</emphasis>. [pause] A cloud is billions of those droplets floating together — a cloud is water, not smoke, and not cotton.
The droplets bump and bunch together. They grow bigger and heavier — until they fall. [pause] That is <emphasis>precipitation</emphasis>: rain, or snow when the air is freezing cold.

Our drop lands high on a mountain and flows downhill — into a stream, into a river, back to the sea. [pause] Up, cloud, down, back. A circle with no end — and the <emphasis>sun</emphasis> is its engine.

Where does water wait between trips? [pause] Most of Earth's water is in the ocean. The rest waits in lakes, rivers, under the ground, and frozen as ice and snow. [pause] And it is always the <emphasis>same water</emphasis>, going round and round — your drop may once have been drunk by a dinosaur!
Put the three process names on the diagram. [pause] Look where the glow is, then tap the right label.
The cycle is labeled! [pause] Now ride along with the drop.
Ride with the drop! At each stop, tap what happens next.
Round the whole circle — well ridden! [pause] One last job: name the process.
Real life clues! For each one, tap the process at work: evaporation, condensation, or precipitation.
You can spot the water cycle everywhere! [pause] Now show what you know.
Not quite. Say the direction. Up as gas — evaporation. Gas becoming droplets — condensation. Falling down — precipitation.
Not quite. Water is never destroyed — it only changes form, or place. Where could it have gone?
Not quite. A cloud is not smoke or cotton — it is billions of tiny water droplets.
Not quite. Follow the circle: up with the sun, into a cloud, down as rain, downhill to the sea.
Not quite. Follow the drop around the circle.
Yes! Going up as invisible gas — evaporation.
Yes! Gas cooling into cloud droplets — condensation.
Yes! Heavy droplets falling — precipitation.
Yes! Warmth lifts it up as gas — evaporation. Water is never destroyed.
Yes! Cold turns the gas into droplets — the drop joins a cloud. Clouds are water, not smoke.
Yes! Heavy droplets fall — precipitation.
Yes! Water always finds the low path — downhill, river, sea. The circle closes!
Yes! Night cold turned water gas in the air into drops — condensation.
Yes! The sun turned it into invisible gas — evaporation. It is not destroyed!
Yes! Falling snow is precipitation — frozen instead of liquid.
Yes! Water gas met the cool mirror and became droplets — condensation.
Yes! The water rose into the air as gas — evaporation.
Yes! Falling rain is precipitation.
The morning puddle is gone by noon. Where did the water go?
What are clouds made of?
What is the engine that keeps the water cycle turning?
High in the cold sky, water gas turns into tiny cloud droplets. What is that process called?
Is the rain that falls today brand-new water?
You can follow a drop around the whole world! [pause] Well done.
Good try! Let's follow the drop once more.
